But I digress.

@ phantaskippy and Ronway:  I'm also backing this game and am extremely excited to get some forum games going!

I also see a lot of commenters who likely haven't even played a game of Story War, yet are basing its merits purely on third party reviews and heresay, when it is very much a subjective game.  Having played (and enjoyed) Story War, I'd like to wildly and somewhat inaccurately compare it to D&D.  Any D&D lovers out there will know that the story telling on top of having a fair and compelling DM will absolutely make or break the experience.  And D&D is a game where "rules" exist more as guidelines, and it really comes down to the imagination of the player when deciding where the game can and can't go.

Story War absolutely hinges on the creativity of its players, and just the same with D&D, when you get the right group of gamers together, it can be an insanely fun and immersive experience (albeit a bit silly).  However, with the wrong group, it definitely falls flat.  But this is nothing new to social games; when the most active part of the game is the players' wit and imagination, it shouldn't be a surprise that a group lacking those things won't find it to be a worthwhile experience.

I don't know; I guess I just see a lot of snap judgements and a lot of people thinking that a game shouldn't exist simply because it isn't their idea of fun.  Even if none of you back Sentinel Conflict, I hope that someday down the line you'll at least try Story War (or other similar social games) with an open minded group.  You'd be surprised with the experiences you could have.  For me, some of the experiences from social games have been the highlights of my year with my friends.

posts.name: Paul
posts.cooked:
Thanks for the feedback everyone, whether you like the idea of Sentinel Conflict or not! I expected that there would be a thread like this when we launched the Kickstarter, and I am glad that it has proceeded in a civil manner :) Here are my answers to some of the questions that came up in this thread:

Q) Who is "Story War: Sentinel Conflict" for?

A) It is for:

*Fans of party/story telling games who want to play one with comic book heroes.

*Fans of Sentinel Comics who want to play a story telling game with characters they love.

*People with casual/non-gamer friends who they want to introduce to Sentinel Comics and eventually convince to play SotM or Tactics.

*Parents who want to introduce Sentinel Comics to their young children.

*Fans of Sentinel Comics who really want a bunch of small art prints with new character art.

 

Q) Why is GTG splitting up the story of Sentinel Comics across multiple different games?

A) We love the world of Sentinel Comics, and believe that there are a few different types of game that work very well with the stories of that universe and, if possible, we would like to make those games and through them tell more stories from Sentinel Comics. Each game is going to appeal to a different core audience, though there will be a lot of overlap.

However, we realize that people are also invested in the story and will want to stay up to date with it. That was one of the motivating factors behind setting Tactics at a different point in the Sentinel Comics timeline; the stories of SotM and Tactics are related, but distinct. With Sentinel Conflict, the game does not provide critical advancement to either story, or contain its own story arc. Instead, it acts as an introduction to the characters and world of Sentinel Comics. We don't want anyone to feel like they have to buy it just for the story.

 

Q) Why did GTG choose Story War as the basis for this party/story telling game?

A) We have played a number of party/story telling games with the "subjectivity mechanic" (popular examples including Apples to Apples and Cards Against Humanity), and we believe that Story War is the best of the genre. (On an amusing note, the back of the original Story War box actually has a quote from Max Tempkin, creator of Cards Against Humanity, saying that Story War is better than CAH). In addition, we felt that the characters, locations, and items format translated very well to the Sentinel Comics universe.

A game that hinges on mechanics, won't really surprise you and is a lot easier to quantify.

What does that even have to do with anything?Do people like games, or do they like games because of who made them?When GtG was SotM everyone who liked SotM liked every game that GtG made.  Because it was one game.I love 2 of their games, that has nothing to do with how I feel about the company, I like the company for completely different reasons.  I like the peoplethat run the company and I like their business model.  I also really like that they support other game-makers when they like the game.If I don't like Spirit Island it won't change that I think it is awesome that they are helping it get made.GtG isn't some mathmatics wizard trying to create only brilliant award winning games.  They are three guys that enjoy telling stories through games who happened to create a comic book world which resonates with a lot of people, and some games that are really fun.  They aren't reinventing gaming, they are just having a good time.  Just let them be themselves, and buy what games you want.

I has everything to do with everything. 

When SotM came out, that was GtG's only game. Then GSF came up for Kickstarter. It had the same type of art and light-hearted feel, and made by the same designer, and many people assumed it would be the same type of game. It was not. Then came Tactics, which was based on a new system, Spirit Island which was designed by someone else, and not Story Wars which is based on another game.

GtG initially gave off this impressions of a designer/publisher. However, it is becomimg clearer and clearer that the desinger part is become less and less. This makes a big difference.  When you hear of a certain desginer, for example, Uwe Rosenberg, Reiner Knizia, Alan Moon, Martinc Wallace, etc., you can usually expect the game to play a particular way. If you like one of their games, there is a decent chance that you will like another. GtG used to be in the category, as a designer, now they aren't.

Publishers are very different. You might know what type of components a game will have (quality wise), but you really don't know how the game will play. Even if you like a previous title, you might not like a new game that is being released.

I think with a project like this, things are changing. That fan base and momentum of being a designer is gone. People will no longer say, "A new GtG game, great I am in," but rather are going to view them as a publisher that is making a new game that might be completely different. Where once you might have said "I love GtG and will get the next game, because I like what they do," this statement changes to "I love SotM, but that has nothing to do with other games."
